issues.legal_issue: A building constructed on watan land after the watan grant does not become watan property merely because it is immovable property standing on that land.
material_facts: The original grant covered the village lands but did not mention the building.
The building was constructed on the granted land after the grant, and the record did not show that it was constructed to provide remuneration for performing the duties of a hereditary office.
The building could be dismantled and its materials removed and sold separately from the land.
issues.conclusion: The building was not watan property and was not immune from attachment on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874 defines watan property as property held, acquired, or assigned to provide remuneration for the performance of duties of a hereditary office. A later-built structure does not acquire the land’s watan character simply because it is immovable property or stands on watan land; the structure must itself satisfy the statutory definition. The Court rejected the approach in Chagla J.’s decision in Second Appeal No. 760 of 1942 that the building was an accession to the land and therefore partook of its character. The fact that a structure is immovable under the Bombay General Clauses Act does not determine whether it is watan property.

rule.if: decree_execution_attachment and structure_built_after_grant and structure_not_created_for_office_remuneration and structure_severable_from_watan_land

predicates.decree_execution_attachment: A creditor sought attachment of a building in execution of a decree against its owner.
predicates.structure_built_after_grant: The building was constructed on the land after the grant that created the watan.
predicates.structure_not_created_for_office_remuner: The building was not shown to have been held, acquired, or assigned to provide remuneration for duties of a hereditary office.
predicates.structure_severable_from_watan_land: The building could be dismantled and its materials removed and sold separately from the land.
predicates.building_not_watan_property: The building does not have the legal character of watan property.

issues.definition: When a building is constructed after a watan grant, was not created to provide remuneration for hereditary-office duties, and is severable from the watan land, it is not treated as watan property in a decree-execution attachment proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A house is not exempt from attachment under the agriculturist protection when its owner is not really dependent on tilling the soil for a living and can maintain himself otherwise.
material_facts: The building belonged to and was occupied by the appellant and was used to store produce and agricultural implements, house farm servants, tether cattle, and provide a residence from which agricultural work was supervised.
The appellant cultivated a home farm through servants and sometimes worked personally in the fields.
The appellant had substantial income from other lands and other sources, and the evidence did not show that the income from other lands resulted from cultivation by him.
The building was sought to be attached in execution of a decree.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was not an agriculturist within the meaning of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the building was not exempt from attachment under section 60(1), proviso clause (c).
issues.legal_principle: Under section 60(1), proviso clauses (b) and (c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, “agriculturist” carries the same meaning in both clauses. A person need not till the land with his own hands, but must be really dependent for his living on tilling the soil and unable to maintain himself otherwise. Clause (c) protects a house belonging to and occupied by an agriculturist as such. The majority adopted the dependency test stated in Parvataneni Lakshmayya v. The Official Receiver of Kistna and referred to Hanmantrao Annarao v. Dhruvaraj Pandurangrao and other High Court decisions in reviewing the competing interpretations. Section 61 concerns exemption of agricultural produce by notification, not the meaning of agriculturist at issue here.

predicates.decree_execution_attachment: A creditor sought attachment of a building in execution of a decree against its owner.
predicates.house_belongs_to_and_is_occupied_by_clai: The claimant owned and occupied the house.
predicates.claimant_not_really_dependent_on_tilling: The claimant had substantial means of maintaining himself apart from tilling the soil, and the evidence did not show that his other land income resulted from cultivation by him.
predicates.agriculturist_house_exemption_unavailabl: The house is not exempt from attachment under the protection for an agriculturist’s house.

issues.definition: In a decree-execution attachment proceeding, an owned and occupied house is not protected by the agriculturist-house exemption when its claimant is not really dependent on tilling the soil for a living.
